analysis.investment_thesis: Anup Engineering is a capex-heavy, project-based B2B industrial equipment maker — the opposite of the predictable, consumer-facing compounders I seek. At 34.8x P/E with negative free cash flow in FY25 despite reporting ₹118 Cr profit, the market is pricing in perfection in a lumpy-order-book business I cannot understand well enough to own.
key_strengths: ROE of 18.9% and ROCE of 18.3% are healthy, touching my 18-22% target range
Operating margins at 17.9% are consistent and expanding — revenue grew from ₹245 Cr to ₹733 Cr in 5 years (24.5% CAGR)
Debt/Equity at 0.25 is technically within my 0.3 ceiling — balance sheet not yet distressed
key_risks: Promoter holding at 40.92% is well below my 55% floor — insufficient owner-operator alignment
FY25 operating cash flow turned negative (-₹7 Cr) despite ₹118 Cr net profit — severe working capital deterioration, FCF was -₹51 Cr
P/E of 34.8x is nearly double my preferred 12-20x band; no margin of safety for a cyclical, project-driven business
red_flags: OCF went from +₹169 Cr in FY24 to -₹7 Cr in FY25 — profit and cash are deeply disconnected
Borrowings surged from zero to ₹158 Cr (balance sheet) while cash collapsed from ₹18 Cr to ₹3 Cr — liquidity rapidly tightening
Promoter stake below 41% with no visibility on trajectory — I will not invest where promoters are not majority anchored
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Anup Engineering is a quality niche industrial business, but it is entirely outside my circle of competence and investment criteria. I built DMart on predictable daily footfall — process equipment for oil refineries and petrochemical plants operates on lumpy multi-crore project orders with 12-24 month execution cycles. When OCF swings from +₹169 Cr in FY24 to -₹7 Cr in FY25 — while reported profits grew to ₹118 Cr — it tells me working capital is being weaponized to show accounting profit while cash bleeds out. That is a pattern I deeply distrust, especially in a business I cannot track at the ground level the way I track retail inventory turns.

The valuation leaves me cold. At 34.8x trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA of 22.4x, the market has already priced in a decade of strong execution. My job is to buy quality at a price where the odds are in my favor, not pay a premium and hope cyclical order books hold. Promoter holding at 40.92% is a structural disqualifier — any promoter who does not hold a controlling majority of their own business has told me something I cannot ignore. The rising borrowings (₹0 to ₹158 Cr in two years) combined with cash near zero creates fragility for what is operationally a good, but not exceptional, franchise. I would need the price to correct 50%+ and the promoter to increase their stake meaningfully before this conversation even begins.
